job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

passage: In our Class 7 social science project, we explored how equality functions in India. We started by visiting a local government school where the mid-day meal scheme is implemented. While the food helps students stay healthy, the primary goal of this program is to ensure that children from all social backgrounds sit together and eat the same meal, thereby reducing caste-based prejudices. Next, we discussed the Right to Vote. We learned that in a democracy, every adult citizen has one vote, regardless of their wealth or social status. A billionaire’s vote is equal to a daily wage worker’s vote. Finally, we examined the law regarding public spaces. We discovered that the Constitution guarantees equality before the law, meaning no shopkeeper or business owner can deny entry or service to anyone based on their caste or religion. These rules ensure that dignity is maintained for every individual. By treating everyone equally in schools, polling booths, and public markets, our democracy aims to provide social justice to all citizens. This project showed us that equality is not just a legal concept but a daily practice that requires us to respect the rights of others in every interaction.

items.evidence: While the food helps students stay healthy, the primary goal of this program is to ensure that children from all social backgrounds sit together and eat the same meal, thereby reducing caste-based prejudices.
items.q: Why does the government run the mid-day meal in schools?
options: To help children of all castes mix as equals
To give food only to the hungriest children
To end caste bias in every school at once
To let each caste group eat in its own row
items.explain: The main goal is that children of all backgrounds sit and eat together, which reduces caste prejudice.

wrong.why: thinks the meal is only to feed hungry children
thinks the meal has already ended caste bias everywhere
thinks separate seating by caste is acceptable

items.evidence: A billionaire’s vote is equal to a daily wage worker’s vote.
items.q: A billionaire and a daily wage worker both vote in an election. What is true of their votes?
options: Each one's vote counts exactly the same
The billionaire's vote counts a little more
The worker's vote counts only if they can read
The one in more groups gets more votes
items.explain: Every adult citizen has one vote, whatever their wealth, so both votes carry equal weight.

wrong.why: thinks rich people's votes count more
thinks only literate people can vote
thinks belonging to more groups gives more votes

items.evidence: We discovered that the Constitution guarantees equality before the law, meaning no shopkeeper or business owner can deny entry or service to anyone based on their caste or religion.
items.q: A shopkeeper in a market refuses to serve a customer because of their caste. What does the law say?
options: The refusal is not allowed under the Constitution
The refusal is allowed, as the shop is private
The refusal is allowed if local people agree
The refusal is allowed only for some castes
items.explain: Equality before the law means no shopkeeper can deny entry or service because of caste or religion.

wrong.why: thinks private shops can refuse people by caste
thinks community agreement can allow separation
thinks the rule covers only some castes

items.evidence: These rules ensure that dignity is maintained for every individual.
items.q: What do these equality rules protect for every person in schools, polling booths and markets?
options: Their right to the same punishment
Their freedom from every law in office
Their claim to equal wealth and land
items.explain: The rules ensure that dignity is maintained for every individual, however rich, poor or of whatever caste.

wrong.why: thinks equality means identical punishment or benefits
thinks officers in office are above the law
thinks equality means everyone gets equal wealth
